title: Land of the Dead
speaker: Zoketsu Norman Fischer
summary: The talk explores the importance of confronting our own darkness and imperfections as a means of finding peace and resolution, using stories from Homer's Odyssey and personal experiences to illustrate this point. It highlights that death is not an escape but rather an unknown limit point of life, and that visiting the "land of the dead" can be a transformative experience that allows us to see our lives and ourselves in a new light. By facing our fears and unresolved emotions, we can cultivate compassion, humility, and patience, leading to a deeper understanding of ourselves and the world around us.

sentences.text: We're trying to figure out whether, at the beginning of the dharma talk, the person giving the talk goes up to offer incense, whether we're all supposed to face the altar or not.
We're working this out.
I've been noticing this for several years.
The forms are so precise, and there's a right way and a wrong way to do it, and there's a million ways to do it, so it's interesting.
Years ago, when I studied with Tetsugen, Bernie Glassman, I went there with my good training from Zen Center.
I think he did this just for me: every day he would change the forms, and every day it was precisely a certain way, but it was different from the way it was yesterday.
So that was a good learning for me.
He was trying to get me out of my rut.
So I've been looking for several years at all these different ways that we are trying to figure out.
We're getting close to figuring out that we're supposed to face the altar.
I think little by little, the majority of people facing the altar is beginning to win the debate that's been going on for several years now.
I was thinking that I probably could give a long disquisition as to why one would face the altar when the incense was offered, and just as long a disquisition as to why one should not.
But I won't do that.
I think we should listen to the wisdom of the majority, and we should all face the altar when the priest goes up to offer the incense.
We're all clear that you face the altar when it's time to bow, right?
But do you begin by facing the altar, or do you wait and turn after the incense is offered?
This is a big point.
But now I think we've worked it out: anyone who does not face the altar when the incense is being offered is making a mistake.
So now we know.

Kate asked me to remind everyone, to clarify for everyone, that when I was recommending that we all pray to Buddha or Guanyin or Tara or whoever we pray to, it would be okay not to pray to anyone in particular.
It's not necessary to pray to someone in particular, which I think makes sense.
And anyway, if you pray to Buddha or Guanyin or Tara or anybody like that, you're also not praying to anyone in particular.
But you might want to not use those names and just pray anyway.
This reminds me of a true story of one close friend in the Dharma that I've been practicing with for about 30 years.
A few years ago he said to me, "After all this time I feel kind of stuck inside, in all the Zen things that I'm doing."
He actually lives in a Dharma center, practicing every day.
He said, "It's not really helping.
I'm still kind of closed inside."
So I said, "Gee, I'm sorry."
I didn't really have anything I could do to help him.
He came back to see me some months later and said, "I think I found a way to get unstuck."
I said, "Great, what are you doing?"
He said, "I'm praying."
I said, "Well, how do you do that?"
He said, "When I really sense the feeling of being stuck inside, I say, 'Please help me, please help me.'" I said, "Is it working?"
And he said, "Yeah.
Somehow when I say, 'Please help me, please help me,' I feel like I'm receiving some help.
And it's helping to open me up inside."
I said, "That's great.
Who are you praying to?"
And he said, "I don't know.
I really don't know who I'm praying to."
So that's like a modern day Zen koan, don't you think?
It's not necessary to pray to anybody in particular.
OK, so this morning I have another story from Tolstoy I thought you'd enjoy.
It's called "Master and Man."
There are three main characters in this story.
The first one is Vasili, who is prosperous, in a small village.
He's not exactly a merchant, but he buys and sells property and owns land and has some serfs and so on.
He's a sort of typical 19th century European bourgeois character, somebody who is very concerned about money and property and getting ahead, his position, his deals.
This is the only thing that he really cares about.
But he's not portrayed as a bad person or a venal person.
He's in fact almost endearing and comical in his utter selfishness and inability to even notice anybody else.
There's something funny about it.
It's so outrageous.
And he's portrayed with a loving touch, I think, by Tolstoy.
He comes originally from a peasant family.
His parents had nothing, so he's very proud of himself that he managed to.
He owns a store and he owns land.
He's very happy about this and very proud of himself, and he's always comparing himself to other people.
Some people have more money than him, and he's thinking that he can continue to make more money and be better than them.
So he's one of the characters in the story.
The second character in the story is someone named Nikita, who is Vasili's servant.
Nikita is a very salt of the earth kind of guy and unfortunately has a small drinking problem.
At least he had in the past.
When he would drink, he wasn't very nice to his wife.
So now he lives apart from his wife.
He lives in Vasili's house, taking care of Vasili, but he sends everything he earns home to his wife and his son.
His wife actually lives with someone else, which he's not thrilled about, but he figures he probably deserves it.
Now he doesn't drink anymore and he's very religious and pious.
But every day it's tough not to drink.
If there's vodka being offered around, it's really tough for him not to take any.
He's a very, very patient and enduring person.
Vasili is constantly cheating him.
Instead of paying him money, he says, "Well, I'll give you this and I'll give you that."
He overvalues the goods that he's giving him so much that he's actually cheating him on his wages.
Even at that, it takes a really long time to pay him.
And he thinks the poor ignorant Nikita has no idea this is going on.
But of course Nikita knows what's going on, and he just shrugs it off.
The third character in the story is a horse, Dapple, who is also a very patient servant.
As you read the story, you get the feeling that Dapple and Nikita are very much alike, very close to one another.
Their communication is very perfect; they really understand each other.
The reason that Dapple is so important in the story is that although the story is 60 pages long, the only thing that happens in the entire story is that they go on a buggy ride.
There's two of them, Vasili and Nikita, with Dapple pulling the sledge.
That's the only thing that happens, more or less, in the whole story.
They're going to a nearby village to transact a business deal that Nikita feels will get him a really good profit.
He wants to get there in a hurry, before the guy who owns the land he wants to buy realizes how much it's really worth, or before somebody else comes and makes a better offer.
So he's quite anxious to get there.
Off they go on the sledge.
And wouldn't you know it, it's winter time in Russia, and it's snowing again.
I mean, it's really snowing.
They shouldn't go, but Vasili's greed is so much that he can't not go.
So off they go in the driving snow.
Vasili is so blinded by his greed, it never occurs to him that this would be a problem.
Of course they get lost in the snow.
The snow is pelting and they can't see anything in front of them.
The road is covered in feet of snow.
They go off into the fields and they're totally lost.
Then they get back on the road and they get to a village, and the village people say, "Oh, this is impossible.
We should stay the night, go in the morning."
"No, no, no, we have to go."
Off they go again and they get lost again.
The whole time Vasili doesn't even think that this is dangerous.
Poor Nikita is constantly having to jump off the sled and run around and find the road.
He comes back exhausted.
Finally they come to a kind of impasse.
Nikita feels like he's going to die.
He's so cold and exhausted that he sits down in the snow to rest.
Vasili unhooks the horse from the sledge and takes off by himself, without any feeling that he's doing something wrong or guilty or anything.
He just takes off.
He's wandering along in the snow and he's trusting that the horse will lead the way.
He has no idea where he's going.
After many hours of wandering, now it's pitch dark, he has had a bout of horrible fear.
But he shrugs, he recovers himself.
He sees something up ahead.
Finally, the village, they approach it.
It turns out to be the sledge.
The horse led him round and round and round in circles and back to the sledge.
Now he looks at the sledge, and Nikita has climbed up on it basically to die.
He says, "Thank God, I'm ready for this."
He's dying, he's dying.
Vasili approaches him and looks at him on the sledge.
Nikita is in a kind of stupor.
He's been dreaming and dreaming of going to heaven or wherever he's going.
He says, "I'm dying.
That's it.
I'm dying.
It's okay.
May Christ save me.
I'm going."
I stupidly forgot to bring the book, because I meant to read you this part.
But I forgot.

It says something like, Vasili looks at him lying on the sledge, and suddenly, with the same kind of decisiveness that he would shake someone's hand in sealing a business deal, he opens up his overcoat, jumps onto the sledge, lies right on top of Nikita and covers him up with his body.
He says to him, "Oh, Nikita, you're not going to die.
I'll warm you up."
But he can't get out any more words, because for some reason he can't understand, he's so moved that he starts weeping.
He lies there on top of Nikita all night long.
There are many pages that I meant to read for you; now you'll all have to read the story, where he's kind of dreaming of his whole life.
He realizes that he can't move his body.
He realizes that he's, in fact, nearly dead himself.
But he's full of joy, because he realizes that Nikita underneath him is warm and is still alive.
Then he says that Vasili, who ran around all the time worried about money and positions and property, didn't know anything about life.
"Who is that man?
But I know.
Now I know about life."
Then he hears someone calling him, and he says, "I'm coming.
I'm coming."
And he's full of joy, full of joy.
And he knows that now he's, and his eyes actually laying on top of Nikita, who's sleeping.
The next morning, we learn, a party comes and finds them and digs them out of the snow.
The sledge is like a big mound of snow.
Vasili is dead.
Dapple is dead.
But Nikita is still alive.
He's lost some toes to frostbite, but he's actually still alive, and he's in the hospital for a few months.
He recovers.
He lives for 20 more years.
At the very end of the story, 20 years later, he also dies.
He's on his deathbed.
He dies under the icons, holding a candle as he had wished.
As he's dying, he thinks to himself, "I'm so happy that I'm dying.
One less mouth to feed for my son and daughter-in-law.
It'll be less of a burden for them."
Then Tolstoy says he's approaching now his death, which with each passing year has been more and more appealing and more and more a pleasant prospect.
The story ends with a line something like: we don't know whether the place where Nikita will wake up tomorrow, after his real death, will be the place of peace that he has been seeking.
We don't know.
But we will all find out soon enough.
That's the last line in the story.
Tolstoy's words are very beautiful, and I regret that I was thinking about something else and forgot to bring the book.
So now I must give my homily on this story.
What can we learn from this story?
The moral of the story is, don't go to Russia in the wintertime.
I actually would like to go to Russia in the wintertime.
I have a friend who's a Russian.
He goes to Russia all the time, and he speaks Russian.
A few years ago, I had a chance to go to Russia.
He invited me to go when he was there in Moscow.
It was the wintertime.
I was really tempted, but I didn't make it that time.
So I hope, before I die, that I can go to Russia in the wintertime.
Anyway, that's, I think, probably the thing that we should most learn from the story.
But also, obviously, it's a beautiful story about redemption.
The funny thing in the story is that Vasili has no revelation, no change of heart, just a sudden decision that has no reason behind it, or no preparation at all.
He just decides to do something.

Somehow, compassion can grab hold of us at any moment and turn our life upside down, so that even for a calculating person like Vasili, sacrificing our lives, even going that far for another, can be seen as something that we really want to do and as a source of joy for us.
That shows you that there are things more important, even than life itself, as Vasili discovered.
And as for Nikita, poor soul that he is, there seems to be a tremendous nobility in his willingness, which you see throughout the story in various small instances that I haven't mentioned.
His tremendous willingness to just simply do whatever needs to be done without complaining, willing to live or die according to whatever happens, whatever is needed.
And this ending of the story is very haunting and profound.
Did Nikita, who worked so hard and so patiently all his life, finally find peace in death?
That we shall all know soon, Tolstoy writes.
So it seems fitting, at the end of the session, to bring up this topic of death.
And also fitting, since tonight we have Florence's priest ordination ceremony, to talk about death at a moment like that.
I used to go to priest ordination ceremonies.
It used to make the end of my hair curl.
In the days when I had hair, it scared the pants off of me.
It's like a funeral ceremony to me.
Florence already told me that she was a little scared.
Maybe she's not now, but she was before.
And I suppose it's rational to be a little scared at a time like that.
Now, this ceremony that we're going to do tonight is simply a ceremony.
It'll take around an hour.
We know how to do it.
We've done it before many times.
It's not a big deal.
First you do this, then you do that, and so forth, like anything else.
On the other hand, it's something a little solemn and scary.
It is like dying to everything that you knew before and waking up the next day who knows where.
Not to overdramatize it, but it is like that.
So just like dying, it's a big step, and you really don't know what's going to happen next.
You have this subject on the table, death, and that's a very lucky thing for me, because I ran out of things to say, yacking all week like this.
Fortunately for me, I brought some writing that I did before that I can now read to you.
It makes it a lot easier.
I don't have to think of anything new to say.
I can read you something that I already wrote before.
This is a little chapter from the book that I just completed called Sailing Home, The Spiritual Odyssey.
Some of you may remember one year here a few years ago I gave some Dharma talks where I talked about the Odyssey and used those talks to make a book.
One of the chapters in the book is called The Land of the Dead.
So I thought, oh, this will be good.
Relevant, cheerful subject, as our session is about to perish, and Florence is going to fall off the deep end.
We might as well talk about death, which as you know is my favorite subject.
So just a very brief introduction.
This chapter comes about maybe half to two-thirds of the way through the book.
The basic idea of the book is that instead of using as my text Dogen or sutras or Buddha's words,
I actually use Homer's Odyssey as a text to talk about spiritual practice.
The reason why I do that, I explain, is that almost all religious texts are hopelessly idealistic.
That's the problem with them, right?
You read about the tremendous purity and enlightenment of the Buddha, and you think, oh no, I could never be like that.
You read about the lofty Dogen words, and you think, ah, that's way beyond me.
But if you read about Odysseus and how he forgets what he's doing in the middle of everything, he falls asleep when he should be awake.
He gives in to his desires and his greed when he should be doing the opposite.
He can't help but boast and brag, and he gets screwed up because of that.
You think to yourself, I can relate to that.
That sounds more like my path.
So I thought it would be good to use the Odyssey as a map of the spiritual journey, which I actually think that it is.
And I think that we're all on some kind of a spiritual journey.
We're practicing with everybody.

If you're a human being, and you're born, and you die, and you're trying to love and be loved, and you're not quite succeeding at that, and you want to find some meaningful life and know yourself, and you're not quite succeeding at that, then you're on a spiritual journey, whether you think so or not, whether you like it or not.
So Odysseus's journey is a journey home.
He's actually fought the battle, and now he's coming home.
And that's the journey, ultimately.
We all leave home so that we can come home.
The ceremony of ordaining, as he's saying, priest, is called tokudou, leaving home.
And you leave home to come to your true home.
So that's the story of Odysseus.
He's trying to come home.
And many things happen to him on the way, many adventures and disasters.
The first part of the book is called leaving home.
The second part is called disaster.
And the third part is coming home.
So this is in the section called disaster.

This takes place, the visit to the land of the dead, right after Odysseus has been visiting Sursa, the sorceress goddess, who they have an adventure with, which fortunately, after some disasters, ends well.
And they have a big feast, which lasts for a year.
They forget what they're doing, and they have a feast.
It lasts for about a year.
And he thinks that after this he's going to go home.
But he finds out from Sursa that actually he's not going home.
He's going to have to go to the land of the dead.
And when he hears about this, the brave, strong Greek hero Odysseus falls down on his bed and he weeps.
He can barely stand it.
But then he recovers, and off he goes.
*So the land of the dead is many things.
It's, first of all, the place of our deepest and most unspeakable fears.
When Odysseus went to the Lotus Eaters, he faced a very subtle enemy, his own lack of awareness, his own forgetfulness, his own kind of losing track of where he was.
But he overcame that.
When he met with the Cyclops, he had to save himself by mastering the art of being nobody.
The disaster of the Aeolian winds showed him the pain of his own deep spiritual ambivalence, which I think we feel too.
And on Sursa's island, he found that he needed to take as allies for his journey his illicit desires and shameful feelings.
And we find that too.
So all this was hair-raising enough, but now he has to go to the land of the dead, and it's much worse.

Because here he has to face the unknown, uncompromising, unappeasable, unnameable force that is literally out of this world, the force of death, the unbeing that wipes away everything we know and everything that is.*
*The land of the dead is also the land of sacrifice, of grief, and of forgiveness.
Because the land of the dead is the land of the long-buried past.
There we are going to re-encounter people that are long gone, whose presence has formed our lives, and there we're going to make a deeper peace with them.
Maybe we thought we already did this work, and maybe we have, but when we encounter these people in the land of the dead, we take the lessons that we've already learned much more deeply to heart.
And we become those people from the past, and they become us.
A visit to the land of the dead is necessary before we can come home.
And we can visit the land of the dead at any time, but in the Odyssean journey it happens later in our lives, when we've already done a lot.
Because now we've been through enough to really be able to incorporate what we learned in the land of the dead in a deeper way, but less romantic, less impassioned way.*
*So Odysseus and his men sail forth till the sun dipped, and all the ways grew dark upon the fathomless, unresting sea.
And they come to a place of utter darkness, a place where the sun cannot shine.
And they beach their ships, and Odysseus follows the instructions given to him by the goddess Sursa.
He digs a pit, and he pours libations around the pit, milk, honey, water, wine, barley.
He sacrifices sheep.
He pours the blood into the pit.
And the idea is that with the blood, the ghosts and shades of the past will come forward, wanting to drink.
And he has to stand guard there with his sword, making them all go away until finally Tiresias comes.
And it's Tiresias, the prophet, who must give Odysseus a prophecy that will enable him to go forward.
That's why he's there.
That's the most important reason why he's there.*
*So all that takes place finally, and Odysseus is terrified as all these ghosts and shades come.
Finally, Tiresias comes and gives his prophecy, the burden of which is this, that Odysseus will make it home, but only after much more suffering.
He will lose all of his men and all of his ships, and he will arrive on Ithaca alone, exhausted.
And when he gets there, he will have further challenges.
He will have to defeat the 108 suitors that are occupying his house.

But Tiresias tells him if he remains patient and steady, if he can keep his mind's wildness in check and communicate this forbearance to those around him whose help he will need, his family members, those closest to him, in the end he will be victorious.
He will bring peace to his household.*
*And above all, Tiresias tells him, you must be always faithful to your journey.
Now comes a long parade of other visitors, and each one comes and tells their tale, because the dead can't lie, so their tales are truthful and go straight to the heart.
And the first one who comes is, guess who, Anteclea, Odysseus' mother.
And she's so happy to see her son alive, but worried that he's there in this place where mortals should never be.
And she tells Odysseus that she died of grief for him, because he went off to Troy.
She didn't know what happened to him.
No one knew where he was, whether he was alive or dead.
And she died of grief.*
And of course Odysseus breaks his heart to hear that.
And now he's full of grief and guilt over this.
And he tries to embrace her.
You can't touch a shade.
A shade gives you the truth, but you can't touch.
And when I read this episode, it made me think of my own mother who died a long time ago, possibly for grief over me, but I hope not.

And after she died, maybe about two or three years after she died, when I was in Tassajara, it was after I no longer lived there, but I would always go in the summers for a visit, stay a week or two, and it was one of those times.
It was a full moon night.
And my mother's shade visited me.
The way shades visit me is through poems.
So as I was writing a poem, my mother actually was writing the poem.
And it was powerful, you know, her words coming through me.
And I felt very close to my mother then.
I had more sympathy and more connection with her actually than I ever had when she was alive.
But just like with Odysseus, it was kind of sad, because I wished that I could have spoken to her and touched her and said something to her, but she wasn't available for that.
She could speak through me, but I couldn't speak to her.

Thinking about my own experiences over the years and hearing from so many people over so many years about their experiences, I've come to appreciate ever more deeply the obvious but too often overlooked importance of the connection that we have with our parents in spiritual practice.

We all know about the psychological aspects of this connection, but the spiritual dimension of the connection to our parents is far less mentioned or understood in the mythic [unclear: "ocean wave"] stories of our lives.
Our parents are more than simply important people.

It's a very intimate and particular kind of experience of father, of mother, that includes and is based on and yet goes far beyond the words and deeds of those actual flesh and blood human beings who occupy these roles in our lives.

And something unspeakably deep is triggered in us with these relationships, and the appreciation and healing of them, because they always require healing regardless of what kind of relationship we have, is, as I think most of us here know, an indelible part of the journey home.
And when we meet our parents in the land of the dead, the connection to them is really poignant and we need these meetings to sustain our onward journey.
Sometimes they take place, as it happened with me and as it happened with Odysseus, after our parents have passed away.
It's luckier if they can take place when our parents are still among the living.
If we're lucky enough to help our parents through the final days of life and into the passage to death, this is a very, very, very important practice.

And I sometimes imagine that when we ourselves are close to death, maybe in the final moments of reverie and dreams like in the Tolstoy story, maybe we will meet our parents more clearly and more vividly than we ever did before.
After Antiklea, a whole bunch of other Greek people come to visit Odysseus, each one bringing a tale about their experiences.
Among them is Achilles, who was the great hero of the Trojan War.
Odysseus is not exactly a hero.
He's sort of a hero, but mostly he's a trickster and a sneaky guy.
He usually gets his way by sneaky tricks.
In fact, it was Odysseus who invented the Trojan horse.
He would think of that.
Achilles, on the other hand, is a strong, brave warrior.
So naturally, he didn't survive the Trojan War.
He was killed in the war, but killed and honored.
This is one of the great things for warriors: to be killed in battle is the greatest thing, to receive great honors and a noble burial.
So Odysseus congratulates Achilles in the Land of the Dead.
"Wow, you must be really proud of yourself, because you are now the most honored person here in the Land of the Dead.
So famous for your bravery, your name honored and revered, known throughout history.
You must be really happy about that."
And Achilles says,
*Let me hear no smooth talk of death from you, Odysseus.
Better, I say, to break sod as a farmhand for some poor countryman on iron rations than to lord it over all the exhausted dead.*
So this is surprising.
Although we all take it for granted that those of us among the living desire life and really don't want to die, this is not entirely true, and we see this also in the Tolstoy story.
Sometimes life gets so burdensome, so troublesome, and it's more the case as one gets older: it's more complicated, more stuff, more responsibility, more people.
Sometimes you think, "Gee, I'd like to have just some peace, forget about all this.
Wouldn't it be nice to die, as if death were a long, beautiful sleep?"
Throughout the Odyssey this happens to Odysseus.
Every now and then he gets burdened with the whole thing, and he says, "Oh, if only I could die, get rid of all this trouble and all this need to journey on."
So we learn here from Achilles that thinking of death as a comfort, as a peaceful nap, is a mistake.

It's a way of avoiding the fact that we absolutely have no idea what death is, and that that's what it is: the unknowable, incomprehensible limit point of life, that which is beyond all reach, which is why death is so impressive to us and so scary.
When Odysseus congratulates Achilles on his noble death, he's imagining that Achilles has found some perfect honor and peace now that his life is done.
But Achilles' message is clear: death is no picnic, Odysseus.
Don't kid yourself.
It's backbreaking, exhausting work.
It is no solution to life's difficulties.
It's the realm of life in which the journey takes place, and death is no escape.
And abandoning our pretty fantasies about death and facing our fear of death's unspeakable unknowingness is a necessity for our life.
This is another thing Odysseus had to go to the land of the dead to find out about.
And he did find out from Achilles.
Nor does death provide us with closure, necessarily.
Another person Odysseus meets is Ajax, somebody he had a dispute with during the Trojan War.
And Ajax actually committed suicide because he was dishonored by Odysseus.
Odysseus feels terrible about this, and he's glad that he sees Ajax in the land of the dead, because now he can make this right.
He goes up to Ajax and says, "Oh, I'm so sorry that happened.
I didn't mean it."
And Ajax kind of looks at him and says, [unclear: "oh, lumber's on without a word"].
Nothing happens.
So a lot of us have relatives or friends, maybe, who are close to death, and we're hoping for a peaceful death for them.
And for ourselves, maybe we can get some closure, some emotional satisfaction in the last weeks of life.
We're thinking maybe we can just have that conversation that will express, heal the wounds if there are wounds, or just express our love.
That one word or gesture that will bring things to a beautiful conclusion.
And sometimes that does happen, actually.
But most of the time, not.
And even if it does happen, it's not a good idea to put too much spin on it, to be too smug about what it all means.
The shades in the land of the dead do not live in a world of peace or closure.
They're still struggling.
And the past, which is dead, is also not static or fixed.
The past is advancing and changing as our life is advancing and changing.
And what we do now, the way we live now, has a tremendous impact throughout all of time and beyond.
I realize this does not make sense, but I think it's true.
It's also very empowering and also a little scary.
But that's one of the lessons that we learn in the land of the dead.
Now, there's a Zen story about the land of the dead, and some of you may have heard me tell this before.
One time a master went with his disciple to a funeral.
The disciple knocked on the coffin and said, "Alive or dead?
Alive or dead?"
And the master said, "I won't say.
I won't say."
The disciple really wanted to know what is life, what is death, and with desperation insisted, "Alive or dead?
Alive or dead?"
And the master said, "I won't say.
I won't say."
And more and more frustrated the disciple got, and he finally said, "If you don't say, I will beat you up, and that's that."
And the master said, "I won't say."
And you do not want to beat up the Zen master.
Bad thing.
